title: Allara Health: what it treats, what it costs, and a doctor by message instead
summary: Allara Health: who you see, $149 a month self-pay (November 2026), insurance, what's extra, and how a $40 FutureClinic doctor visit by message compares.
body_markdown:
Allara Health and FutureClinic both offer PCOS care online: Allara as a monthly program of scheduled video visits with a medical provider and a registered dietitian, FutureClinic through a physician you message, with no subscription required. Allara's Complete Care costs $149 a month self-pay as of November 2026, while FutureClinic costs $40 for the best-fit doctor, or a chosen doctor's listed price, typically $20 to $100.


## What is Allara Health and what does it treat?


Allara Health is a telehealth program for complex hormonal, metabolic, and gynecological conditions, calling itself a women's specialty care platform on its[FAQ page](https://www.allarahealth.com/faq) . It treats PCOS, insulin resistance, endometriosis, Hashimoto's thyroiditis, hypothyroidism, primary ovarian insufficiency,[menopause](https://futureclinic.com/blog/midi-health-vs-futureclinic-menopause-care-cost-comparison) , PMDD, uterine fibroids, fertility issues, weight concerns, fatigue, irregular periods, acne, hair loss, and excess body hair.


## How does Allara Health work?


Allara runs care through scheduled video visits with one medical provider (a board-certified OB-GYN, endocrinologist, or women's health nurse practitioner matched by location, insurance, and symptoms) and one registered dietitian who stay with you every visit. On its[how it works page](https://www.allarahealth.com/how-it-works) , care starts with a 30-minute provider video visit and a 45-minute dietitian video visit, then hormone and metabolic testing, a care plan (supplements, nutrition, exercise, stress, medicine), and check-ins every one to two weeks, or as often as your provider recommends. The[Allara app](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/allara/id1660816488) and[services page](https://www.allarahealth.com/services) include messaging and a Patient Concierge between visits. Many patients stay prescription-free, and Allara does not replace your in-person OB-GYN or primary care.


## How much does Allara Health cost with and without insurance?


Without insurance, Allara Health's Complete Care Program (medical and nutrition) costs $149 a month and its Nutrition Program $125 a month, as of November 2026; with an in-network plan, Allara adds no membership fee, though copays, coinsurance and deductibles may apply. Per Allara's[insurance and pricing page](https://www.allarahealth.com/insurance-pricing) and[terms](https://www.allarahealth.com/terms-conditions) , plans bill monthly with no long-term commitment, auto-renew, and are generally non-refundable; labs and medicine are extra.


Allara is in-network with select insurance plans; its pricing page names Aetna, Blue Cross Blue Shield, Cigna, UnitedHealthcare and GEHA on select plans. On its[prescriptions page](https://www.allarahealth.com/prescriptions) , off-label metformin, off-label spironolactone, Contrave, and GLP-1s (semaglutide, tirzepatide, liraglutide) go to a local or mail-order pharmacy (Allara Rx also lists GLP-1s), while Allara Rx custom skin topicals start at $29 per 30-day supply as of November 2026.


## What does PCOS diagnosis and treatment involve?


There is no single test for PCOS: a doctor uses your history, an exam and blood tests to rule out other causes, and the first-line medicine for irregular periods and high-androgen signs is a combined birth control pill. The[Office on Women's Health](https://www.womenshealth.gov/a-z-topics/polycystic-ovary-syndrome) notes PCOS affects 1 in 10 women of childbearing age and is a common treatable cause of infertility. Under the[2023 International Evidence-based Guideline](https://assets.monashivf.com/assets/Summary-International-evidence-based-guideline-for-the-assessment-and-management-of-polycystic-ovary-syndrome-2023.pdf) , adult diagnosis requires two of three features: high androgens, irregular or absent ovulation, and polycystic ovaries on ultrasound or raised AMH (no ultrasound is needed when irregular cycles and high androgens are both present). Blood tests rule out thyroid disease (TSH), high prolactin and non-classic congenital adrenal hyperplasia (17-hydroxyprogesterone). Diabetes, heart disease, sleep disorders, depression and anxiety are all more common with PCOS, so the guideline recommends screening for them.


Per[NICHD](https://www.nichd.nih.gov/health/topics/pcos/conditioninfo/treatments) , many treatments, metformin among them, are not FDA approved specifically for PCOS but treat its symptoms. The[2023 guideline](https://assets.monashivf.com/assets/Summary-International-evidence-based-guideline-for-the-assessment-and-management-of-polycystic-ovary-syndrome-2023.pdf) finds no single diet or exercise plan best, and no one combined pill, though it prefers lower-dose pills with fewer side effects.[Combined pills](https://futureclinic.com/blog/birth-control-online-without-a-subscription) are first-line for irregular cycles and androgen signs, metformin targets metabolic features, anti-androgens such as spironolactone have a limited role, for use when other treatments don't work or aren't suitable, and[anti-obesity medicines](https://futureclinic.com/blog/weight-loss-medication-online-no-membership-fee) may be considered. By message, a physician can review history and photos, order labs, follow up, and prescribe non-controlled medicines if your doctor decides it's right for you; an ultrasound needs an in-person visit.
